drills.q: What is the rough memory-per-parameter cost of full fine-tuning with Adam, and what does it total for a 7B model?
drills.a: ~16-18 bytes/param (bf16 weight+grad, fp32 master weight, fp32 momentum+variance) -> ~112-140GB for 7B, before activations.

drills.q: Write the LoRA forward pass formula and state how B and A are initialized.
drills.a: h = Wx + (alpha/r) B A x. A: small random init. B: zero init, so delta W = 0 at the start of training.

drills.q: A manager wants to fine-tune a model on internal docs so it 'knows the product.' What do you recommend instead, and why?
drills.a: Recommend RAG: knowledge injected via fine-tuning is frozen at training time, goes stale as docs change, requires a full retrain per update, and gives no provenance. Retrieval updates immediately and can cite the source chunk.

drills.q: Compute the LoRA parameter count for a 4096x4096 weight matrix at rank 16, and compare to full fine-tuning of that matrix.
drills.a: Full FT: 4096x4096 ~= 16.8M params. LoRA r=16: 4096x16 + 16x4096 = 131,072 params -- about a 128x reduction.

drills.q: Name the three QLoRA-specific tricks and what each one buys you.
drills.a: NF4 (4-bit bins at normal quantiles, fits weight distribution better than linear INT4), double quantization (quantizes the block scaling constants themselves, ~0.37 bit/param saved, ~3GB on 65B), paged optimizers (page Adam state to CPU RAM on gradient-checkpointing memory spikes instead of OOMing).

drills.q: Explain mechanically why a merged DoRA adapter adds zero inference latency despite decomposing magnitude and direction separately.
drills.a: Both the magnitude vector and the LoRA-adapted direction are linear compositions on the frozen base weight; the whole decomposition folds back into a single weight matrix before serving, identical in cost to a plain merged LoRA adapter -- no extra runtime computation.

drills.q: A team fine-tunes a support model and general coding ability regresses afterward. Diagnose and give two mitigations.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting: training pushed weights toward the narrow distribution and degraded unreinforced capability. Mitigate with LoRA/QLoRA instead of full FT, cap training epochs, mix in general instruction data, and evaluate on an out-of-domain probe set before shipping.

drills.q: Your LoRA adapter at rank 16 plateaus below full-FT quality on a code-generation task. What two changes would you try before concluding LoRA has hit a ceiling?
drills.a: Raise rank (e.g. to 32-64, since 2025 research favors intermediate ranks for complex tasks) and expand target_modules to all linear layers including MLP up/down/gate projections, not just attention Q/V, since code tasks stress MLP capacity.

drills.q: Design the fine-tuning approach for a ticket-triage model given ~5,000 historical labeled tickets. What eval-set mistake would silently hide a real production regression here?
drills.a: Fine-tune with QLoRA at r=16-32 targeting all-linear, after checking whether few-shot prompting already suffices. The eval mistake: using a random split instead of a temporally-held-out slice -- ticket types and routing categories drift over time, so a random split from the same historical window can show 95% accuracy while production routing has already shifted.

drills.q: Explain how vLLM's multi-LoRA serving avoids the cost of one full model copy per customer adapter, and what happens if you naively merge each adapter instead.
drills.a: The base model stays resident once; each adapter is applied per-request as a small batched matmul, so throughput stays near base-model speed across hundreds to thousands of adapters. Naively merging each adapter into the base produces a full-size model copy per adapter, reintroducing the storage/swap cost multi-adapter serving exists to eliminate.

drills.q: A colleague wants to fine-tune purely to shrink a long production system prompt for cost reasons. Legitimate use of fine-tuning or not, and what's the catch?
drills.a: Legitimate -- it's distilling a behavior/format pattern into weights, not injecting facts, which is exactly what fine-tuning is good at. The catch: if the few-shot examples embedded specific facts (prices, policies) rather than pure formatting/behavior, fine-tuning on them re-introduces the knowledge-injection failure mode by the back door.

drills.q: State the data-quality rule of thumb for deciding whether you have enough data to fine-tune, and the risk of ignoring it.
drills.a: 1,000 curated, diverse examples typically beat 100,000 noisy ones. Ignoring it and training on a large but low-diversity or inconsistent set causes overfitting to incidental patterns, which a held-out split from the same source won't reveal -- only an out-of-domain probe set catches it.
